title: I Built My Own Smart Home Security System—No Subscription Required
author: Nena Farrell
text:
All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.No one wants to worry about a break-in. But no one wants to end up paying fees every month just to check their video doorbell feed or find out their window was broken, and most smart security systems (even the original ones that weren't touted as smart!) rely on your fear to have you paying month after month for the promise of catching burglars and stopping intruders for you.These systems do work, and they can give you a lot of peace of mind. This comes with a hefty price tag, though, and plenty of people would be more than happy with a system they build themselves sans monthly fees. If you're not interested in a system that will call the police or fire department if you don't respond fast enough to something that turns out to be minor, or don't want to have strangers looking through your security cameras at your property, I'm here to help with that.This guide collects a handful of our favorite smart home security accessories that won't paywall you left and right, and will give you local storage options for video so you aren't locked into the cloud. This way you can build the system that works for you. Here's everything I recommend if you want smart home security without the subscriptions.Table of ContentsWhat Exactly Is a Smart Home Security System?What Do Smart Security Systems and Subscription Services Get You?Do You Need a Smart Security Setup With a Subscription?Best Subscription-Free Smart LocksBest Subscription-Free Video DoorbellBest Subscription-Free Security CamerasBest Subscription-Free Motion SensorsSome Subscription-Free Door and Window SensorsWhat Exactly Is a Smart Home Security System?Smart security systems can look like whatever you want, in my opinion, but there are a lot of starter kits you've probably seen. Smart-home brands like Abode and SimpliSafe have starter packs you've likely seen before with motion sensors, door sensors, and security hubs that sound an alarm when one of those sensors is triggered.Featured VideoSecurity Cameras That Keep Your Footage Local—No Subscription NeededBut smart home security can go way beyond that. Most systems let you add on cameras and even video doorbells to monitor movement around your home and catch people at your door who shouldn't be there. (This is also a handy way to know when it’s a package delivery or another random salesperson.) These systems are usually modular and customizable, whether you DIY or go with a brand. Overall, the goal is to protect and monitor your home through motion sensors and video feeds.Home security brands usually have various subscription options and some kind of self-monitored, subscription-free tier, but you usually lose out on a variety of features to encourage you to subscribe.What Do Smart Home Security Systems and a Subscription Get You?I remember running into the issue of paywalled features for the first time a few years ago when I was testing Abode's smart lock. I liked the lock, but I woke up to unclear notifications that happened in the dead of night. Had the lock been hacked? Had it sensed itself being manually opened when we were asleep? There was no way to tell because Abode’s base level would only tell me the lock was interacted with without explaining how. I signed up for the Abode membership that day to be able to review the events, and luckily it was just a loss of Wi-Fi connection and reestablishment that happened within a minute of each other. Crisis averted.The main thing that subscription services paywall is video storage, which allows you to review past events at your home. Sometimes it can also be notifications, whether that's the type of notification or the ability to review notification history. What is or is not paywalled largely depends on the brand and its offerings. Professional live monitoring, however, is almost always paywalled, whether that's an agent calling police when an alarm has been triggered or an agent reviewing flagged footage (e.g., motion alerts) to either notify you of a situation or call emergency services on your behalf. That’s one thing you can't DIY—if you’re on vacation or otherwise not able to call police if there's an issue, you're out of luck.Base stations from home security companies like ADT, SimpliSafe, and Vivint will act as a smart-home hub to connect and control sensors and other devices, and be able to sound an alarm. It might have a keypad that you can use to arm and disarm the system too.Most PopularGearMeta's Muse Is Better at Surveilling Than Helping MeBy Reece RogersHow To and AdviceWhat ChatGPT Thinks It Knows About You Is Affecting Its Answers. Here’s How to Change ThatBy David NieldGearDyson Won’t Say What’s Wrong With Its CameraJet ToothbrushBy Jeremy WhiteGearI Printed a Shovel, Earrings, and Everything in Between With This 3D PrinterBy Kat MerckA lot of subscription services also have a higher tier that gives you an on-staff specialist who will review live footage if a camera is triggered, or even use the microphone to speak to an intruder. It's a useful feature if it's something you're worried about, but those subscriptions can cost as much as a casual grocery trip each month.Do You Need a Smart Home Security System Starter Kit?Courtesy of SimpliSafeSimpliSafe8-Piece Wireless Home Security System$229 $209 (9% off) Amazon$350 $100 (71% off) Best Buy (Outdoor)$230 $130 (43% off) Best Buy (Indoor)You don't need a formal, branded home security kit to protect your home, but if you're interested in window and motion sensors that will trigger and sound an alarm, you might want one. You can buy a kit and even have a brand representative come and install the devices for you. (But as someone who's seen the bill for those, I'd recommend installing everything yourself, since it has to be connected to your phone and personal accounts anyway.)If you're just looking to know who's at your door, get alerted when a window is opened, or prove you have trespassers with video footage, DIY-ing your own system with a handful of devices that fit the needs you're looking for is a fine solution. Personally, I worry most about my front door, while someone else might worry about trespassers in their backyard. Buying accessories à la carte allows you to get exactly what you want without paying extra.Best Subscription-Free Security Devices to Build Your Own SystemBest Subscription-Free Smart LocksSmart locks are my most-used smart-home item by far. Having a smart lock makes it so easy for my entire family to access our home, including my 4-year-old, who has memorized the code. Smart locks make it easy to confirm your door is locked when it should be, and you can see the access history to know who's opening it and when. These are two of my favorite options that don't require any sort of subscription to get event history in an app, but you will need to buy a separate Wi-Fi hub or bridge for both if you want remote access. However, that's a one-time purchase instead of a forever one.Photograph: Nena FarrellPhotograph: Nena FarrellAqaraSmart Lock U50$120 AmazonThis is my favorite smart lock. It's easy to install and use, and it doesn't require a subscription, but you will need to use a hub like the Aqara M100 ($30) to get Wi-Fi control. It works perfectly well with Bluetooth-based control, though, if you don't want to purchase any extras. There are other Aqara products you can get for around your house if you wanted to create a security system all through a single app, though Aqara's app isn't the best.
Photograph: Nena FarrellPhotograph: Nena FarrellPhotograph: Nena FarrellLevelLock Pro$349 Amazon$349 Home Depot$349 LevelLevel's smart locks are the most discreet I've tried; you'd never think this door is smart from looking at it, but it is. Level does sell its Connect Wi-Fi Bridge ($79) separately, along with a separate Keypad ($79), which I recommend for creating codes that friends and family members can use. Level doesn't make any other products beyond locks if you wanted a one-brand setup, though.
Best Subscription-Free Video DoorbellMost video doorbells have a no-subscription option, but you'll usually lose out on video storage, so you can't scroll back and see what happened when an alert went off. You'll also miss out on some notification types and features like package detection. I think doorbells and video cameras are impacted the most by the loss of features without a subscription, since so many then lose the ability to show you what happened that day or who rang the bell. These video doorbells below get around that with local storage options, so your footage is saved to a microSD card rather than the cloud. However, if you don't properly secure the camera, you could lose the footage and camera both, since all data is stored in the device.Photograph: Simon HillEufyVideo Doorbell E340$150 Amazon$150 Best Buy$149 WalmartEufy's E340 is our favorite subscription-free doorbell since there's a local storage option, allowing you to skip a subscription fee to have video you can review later on. There's up to 8 GB on the device, and you can add a microSD card for up to 128 GB. There are two cameras in it, so it can spot people as easily as packages on your doorstep, and it works with Google Home and Amazon Alexa (but not Apple).
Photograph: Simon HillReolinkVideo Doorbell$120 Amazon$120 $100 (17% off) WalmartAnother local-recording option is the Reolink Video Doorbell. It supports Power over Ethernet for a more secure connection, and the doorbell records footage to a microSD card. You'll also get person detection and custom zone support without needing a subscription. It does require a wired connection, and also works with Amazon Alexa and Google Home, but not Apple.
Best Subscription-Free Security CamerasSimilar to video doorbells, you'll often run into subscription fees for security cameras in order to store footage in the cloud and review it. Instead, choose one of these cameras for the inside or outside of your home that allows local storage, so you can live subscription-free. We've got a whole guide to subscription-free security cameras if you want more options. Again, make sure the camera is secured so you don't lose the camera and footage in one go.Photograph: Simon HillPhotograph: Simon HillPhotograph: Simon HillEufyEufyCam S4$350 Amazon$800 Amazon (2-Cam Kit)$1,400 Amazon (4-Cam Kit)$1,400 Eufy (4-Cam Kit)Eufy's back again with a local storage option, this time for the outdoor camera. It's expensive, especially if you purchase the four-pack, but WIRED reviewer Simon Hill says it's the most versatile and feature-packed local security camera system. There's 32 GB of built-in storage that you can expand to 256 GB with a microSD card. It's best when paired with Eufy's HomeBase S380 for local face recognition and more local storage on the base.
Photograph: Simon HillTP-LinkTapo Wire-Free MagCam (Battery)$120 $77 (36% off) TP-Link$136 $115 (15% off) Amazon (2-Pack)$250 $200 (20% off) Best Buy (3-Pack)If you're looking for something on the cheaper end, the Tapo line from TP-Link is WIRED reviewer Simon Hill's budget-conscious pick for a subscription-free security camera. He says it's some of the best-quality local recording cameras you can get for a cheaper price. You can add a microSD card to these cameras for up to a whopping 512 GB of local storage. You can also choose a two-camera kit that comes with an indoor hub and microSD card.

The Tapo 120 is WIRED reviewer Simon Hill's top pick for an indoor camera, but he says the cheaper C110 is also a good choice. It also allows for local storage up to 512 GB with a microSD card.
Best Subscription-Free Motion SensorsMotion sensors are a primary feature of most smart home security kits, but they usually don't need a subscription fee to work—when a sensor is triggered, the base station will sound an alarm. The subscription really just allows for an agent to call your local authorities if the alarm sounds; otherwise, you'll just get a notification on your phone to find out if someone's where they shouldn't be.If you're looking for motion sensors that will activate smart-home features like turning on a switch when you walk by, these aren't it. These are designed to set off an immediate alarm when any motion is detected. Check out our guide to the Best Motion Sensors for more ideas there.Photograph: Simon HillPhotograph: Simon HillPhotograph: Simon HillPhotograph: Simon HillLetwesafRadar Motion Alarm System$220 AmazonThis is a radar system best for large properties, since it has a range of up to half a mile. It doesn't need Wi-Fi or an app: You just pair the receiver and detector, and you're ready to go. It'll alarm when any person or animal is detected, so set it up somewhere no one should be; WIRED reviewer Simon Hill suggests it for protecting the exterior of your home, or even your RV on a camping trip (or if it's left alone in a corner of your yard most of the year).
Photograph: Simon HillPhotograph: Simon HillPhotograph: Simon HillKinisiumKini SafeAlert Wi-Fi Motion Sensor$80 AmazonWIRED reviewer Simon Hill recommends this motion sensor to protect cupboards and cabinets that have valuables or dangerous items in them. The sensors inside detect movement in any direction. It only connects to 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi, but allows for a ton of specific configurations and alerts that you can set up over the mobile app or on your web browser.
Some Subscription-Free Door and Window SensorsThis is another popular feature of smart home security kits. It's great for getting an alert on a door that doesn't have a smart lock, or wouldn't be regularly locked. Even better for windows or sliding doors that have no other way to alert you if they're opened.I haven't tested these yet, but I've tested other products from these brands and have liked the experience, and share more about both below. They're next on my testing list for this story.Most PopularGearMeta's Muse Is Better at Surveilling Than Helping MeBy Reece RogersHow To and AdviceWhat ChatGPT Thinks It Knows About You Is Affecting Its Answers. I found the smart lock reliable and consistent, and testing these sensors is top of my list for this story's next update.
Courtesy of IkeaIkeaMyggbett Door/Window Sensor, Smart$12 IkeaWant to go really cheap? Ikea's smart home system is super affordable and Matter compatible, but the app won't show you a history of actions the way other apps can. I've tested other Ikea smart-home devices and found them plenty reliable, too, so I'm hopeful to see similar results with the Myggbett.
